title: How to Break Down Tasks with ADHD (So You Can Start)

scenes.text: Clean the apartment. Do your taxes. Write the report. Those aren't tasks. They're projects pretending to be tasks. And for an A D H D brain, that's often why they never get started. Let's fix that, by breaking them down the right way.

When a task is vague, your brain has to plan it before it can start it. Planning runs on executive function, which is often the exact thing that's harder with A D H D. So the task just sits there. Breaking it down does the planning ahead of time, so starting is the only job left.

Here are three rules for a breakdown that actually works. One. Every step starts with a verb you can picture yourself doing. Open, write, pick up, send. Two. Each step takes about two to ten minutes. If it's longer, split it again. Three. The first step should be so easy it feels almost silly.

items.text: 1. Start with a verb you can picture

scenes.text: Let's try it. Clean the kitchen becomes this. Put all the dishes in the sink. Load the dishwasher. Wipe the counters. Take out the trash. Sweep the floor. Each step is small, clear, and has an end.

steps.text: Put all the dishes in the sink

scenes.text: But what if even the first step feels too big? Then go smaller. Put the dishes in the sink can become, pick up one cup. No step is too small. If it gets you moving, it counts.

A few more tips. Write the steps down, so your working memory doesn't have to hold them. Add a rough time to each step, which can help with time blindness. Look only at the next step, and hide the rest if they feel like too much. And celebrate every step you check off.
